newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomber faces formal sentencing.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomber faces formal sentencing.

text.p: Convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh will be formally sentenced to death on Thursday amid reports that he will use the occasion to break his long silence about the case.

In June, a jury found the 29-year-old Gulf War veteran guilty and sentenced him to die for the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City that killed 168 people.

On Thursday, U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch is to formally impose the death sentence. Some of the relatives of people who died in the bombing have said they will be in the courtroom when the sentence is pronounced.

McVeigh was stoic and almost completely silent throughout the 11-week trial, showing no emotion during days of sometimes heartwrenching testimony about the impact the bombing had on survivors and people who lost loved ones in the bombing.
In an interview with the Buffalo News published Wednesday, McVeigh said he would speak at his formal sentencing and complained about his lead attorney Stephen Jones.
He did not testify during the trial and when he did speak in court it was usually only one-word answers to the trial judge.
In a telephone interview from a federal prison in suburban Denver, McVeigh said Jones "screwed up" his case and should be dropped from handling the appeals process.

"The truth is this guy only succeeded in getting the death sentence and now he doesn't want to let go," McVeigh said. "He screwed up badly, but I'm not bitter. I only want him off my appeal," he told the newspaper.
Jones said in a statement that he would not discuss his conversations with his client, whom he said was "under great personal stress on the eve of the imposition of the death sentence."
Jones said he would remain McVeigh's attorney until and if the court appointed someone else and said he was legally obligated to stay on the case through the first appeal.

It is not known if McVeigh will try to defend his actions when he addresses the court on Thursday. He told the newspaper he showed no emotion during the trial because he was trying to be "a total gentleman in the courtroom when people called me a coward."
McVeigh's co-defendant Terry Nichols is scheduled to go on trial Sept. 29 in Denver, although his attorneys are seeking a change of venue to San Francisco.
Matsch said he would decide soon on the change of venue request, which prosecutors oppose.
